items.text: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients 4.
items.why: Hypothesizes dot products push softmax into regions with vanishing gradients.

items.text: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)).
items.why: Shows learned and sinusoidal positional encodings yield nearly identical performance.

items.text: We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.
items.why: Speculates sinusoidal encodings facilitate extrapolation to unseen sequence lengths.

items.text: For the base models, we used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints, which were written at 10-minute intervals.
items.why: Reveals single-model evaluation relies on averaging multiple training checkpoints.

items.text: We estimate the number of floating point operations used to train a model by multiplying the training time, the number of GPUs used, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU 5.
items.why: Explains FLOPs were estimated via hardware capacity approximations.

items.text: While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.
items.why: Reports ablation result that performance degrades when using too many heads.

items.text: This suggests that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial.
items.why: Infers dot product may be an overly simplistic compatibility function.
